title: Whether a reading lesson takes speech
statement: Whether a reading lesson should take spoken answers at all is unsettled: one course's lesson designs rule out voice input, while the engine it runs on asks for speech.
example: Every one of the lesson designs' 20 structural gate checks repeats 'no voice input'.
detail: The reading rule pack that the course renderer's authoring pipeline reads records a live conflict: the curriculum's master lesson spine says there is no speaking, and every one of its 20 structural gate checks repeats no voice input, while the engine ships speaking tasks, a say-back on every vocabulary card and speech-to-text scoring (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/authoring/inputs/rule-packs/reading-g3.json`, line 243). The pack follows the engine because that is what shipped, and records the conflict so the pipeline never presents it as settled. The curriculum's lesson-components sheet of 2026-08-06 says of its vocabulary step that there is no speaking and that understanding is checked by a multiple-choice question (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/pedagogy/example-lesson-components-2026-08-06.md`, line 22).

evidence.quote: The team's master spine says 'there is no speaking' and every one of their 20 structural gate checks repeats 'no voice input'. This engine ships speak nodes, a say-back on every vocabulary card and STT scoring. That is a live CONFLICT, not a gap, and it needs a ruling.
recorded so the pipeline never presents the conflict as settled
There is no speaking; understanding is checked by the MCQ.
